Front: What is the multi-stage recommendation pipeline architecture?
Back: Retrieval (two-tower ANN, <10ms, ~1000 candidates) -> Scoring (DCN V2/DeepFM, 10-50ms, ~200 scored) -> Reranking (LLM semantic, 100-300ms, ~50 reranked, optional) -> Business Rules (diversity/policy, <5ms, final top-K).

Front: What is the "killer framing" for recommendation system evolution?
Back: The evolution from FTRL to deep learning to LLM-enhanced is not replacement but accumulation -- each layer serves where it adds unique value. The question is never 'which model' but 'which model at which stage for which latency budget.'

Front: How does a two-tower model work for recommendation retrieval?
Back: Two separate neural networks encode queries (user context) and items into the same d-dimensional embedding space. Relevance is approximated by dot product, enabling sub-linear ANN retrieval over millions of items. Item embeddings are pre-computed and indexed.

Front: What is the fundamental limitation of two-tower models?
Back: The representation bottleneck: all query-item interaction reduces to a single scalar (dot product). "Red running shoes" vs "red hiking boots" may score similarly because most embedding dimensions align. Token-level alignment is lost -- cross-attention captures this but cannot be pre-indexed.

Front: What is FTRL and why is it still used in modern recommendation systems?
Back: FTRL (Follow The Regularized Leader) is an online learning algorithm with per-coordinate learning rates and L1 sparsity for real-time model updates on billions of sparse features. Critical for auction systems where the world changes hourly. No neural architecture matches its speed + sparsity + online adaptivity for CTR prediction.

Front: How do FTRL's per-coordinate learning rates work?
Back: FTRL maintains per-feature accumulators n_i (sum of squared gradients). Effective learning rate = alpha / (beta + sqrt(n_i)). A rare feature (advertiser-keyword cross, updates once/day) gets much higher learning rate than a global CTR feature (updates millions of times). Critical when sparsity spans 6+ orders of magnitude.

Front: How does FTRL achieve true sparsity?
Back: At prediction time, FTRL checks if |z_i| <= lambda_1 -- if so, w_i = 0 exactly. This yields truly sparse models (90%+ zeros at serving time), critical for memory efficiency with billions of features. SGD and Adam produce small-but-nonzero weights; only L1 proximal gives exact zeros.

Front: What is DeepFM and how does it differ from Wide & Deep?
Back: DeepFM jointly trains a factorization machine (second-order interactions) and deep network (higher-order) with shared embeddings, eliminating manual feature engineering. Unlike Wide & Deep (requires manual cross features for wide component), DeepFM automates interaction discovery entirely.

Front: What is DCN V2 and how does it improve over DeepFM?
Back: DCN V2 replaces DeepFM's fixed factorization with learnable cross layers: x_{l+1} = x_0 * (W_l * x_l + b_l) + x_l. Stacking L cross layers captures up to (L+1)-order interactions with O(d) params per layer. Adds mixture-of-experts and low-rank decomposition. Outperforms DeepFM on large-scale CTR benchmarks.

Front: What is the in-batch negative sampling bias problem?
Back: In-batch negatives are sampled proportional to item popularity (popular items appear in more batches). This teaches the model "popular items are irrelevant" -- opposite of reality. Yi et al. fix: corrected logit = s(q,i-) - log(p_j), where p_j is sampling probability.

Front: What is log-Q correction for sampling bias?
Back: Yi et al. (2019): subtract log(p_j) from negative logits, where p_j = count(j)/sum(counts). This ensures rare items are treated as "harder" negatives (they deserve higher penalty when incorrectly matched), debiasing toward uniform item distribution.

Front: What is the mixed negative sampling recipe for two-tower training?
Back: 70% in-batch negatives (with log-Q correction) + 20% hard negatives (top-K by embedding similarity, filtered by label) + 10% random (from global catalog, for calibration). Yang et al. showed mixed outperforms any single strategy by 4-6% Recall@K.

Front: Why are hard negatives important and what is the false-negative problem?
Back: Hard negatives (similar embedding but different intent) force fine-grained discrimination -- 1 hard negative approximates 100 random negatives in gradient signal. Problem: a "hard negative" might actually be relevant but uninteracted. Mitigations: impression-based mining, confidence filtering, label smoothing (0.05-0.1).

Front: What is position bias and the Position-Based Model (PBM)?
Back: P(click | item, position) = P(relevant | item) * P(examine | position). Users click top positions regardless of relevance. Without correction, models learn "position 1 is good" rather than "this item is good." IPW weights each sample by 1/P(examine|position).

Front: How does IPW correction work for position-biased training data?
Back: Weight each training sample: w_k = 1/P(examine|position k). Click at position 1 (P(examine)~0.95) gets weight ~1.05. Click at position 8 (P(examine)~0.25) gets weight ~4.0. A click at position 8 is much more informative about true relevance (user made effort to look).

Front: What is the IPW variance problem and how do you solve it?
Back: Items at position 20 (P(examine)~0.05) get weight 20x, amplifying noise. Solution: clipped IPW -- w_k = min(1/P(examine|k), max_weight), typical max_weight=10-20. Trades some bias for much lower variance. Plot MSE vs clip threshold on held-out randomized data to find optimum.

Front: What are the three approaches to propensity estimation?
Back: (1) Randomization (gold standard): shuffle 1-5% of results, measure position-dependent click rates. (2) Regression discontinuity: exploit natural position breaks (above/below fold). (3) EM algorithm: jointly estimate examination and relevance from observational data without randomization.

Front: How does multi-objective ranking balance conflicting goals?
Back: Approaches: (1) Scalarization: weighted sum (simple but arbitrary). (2) Constrained optimization: maximize primary subject to thresholds on secondary (principled -- thresholds are business decisions). (3) MMR reranking: lambda*relevance - (1-lambda)*max_similarity (natural diversity). (4) Pareto set generation.

Front: Why is constrained optimization preferred over weighted scalarization for multi-objective ranking?
Back: Scalarization weights are arbitrary, can't find non-convex Pareto solutions, and mix model decisions with business decisions. Constrained optimization separates: ML optimizes within constraints, business sets constraints (explicit thresholds). This organizational separation is critical in production.

Front: When does traditional ML outperform LLMs for ranking?
Back: Traditional ML wins for: calibrated P(click) for auctions (LLMs don't calibrate), 100K candidates in <10ms (LLMs 1000x slower), tabular behavioral features, real-time adaptation (FTRL). LLMs win for: cold-start understanding, semantic query-item matching.

Front: What are the four LLM integration points for recommendation, ranked by ROI?
Back: (1) Offline feature generation -- highest ROI, zero runtime cost, amortized once per item. (2) Query understanding -- medium ROI, adds 50-100ms for complex queries. (3) Reranking top-K -- high ROI but selective, adds 100-300ms. (4) Explanation generation -- medium ROI, cacheable.

Front: What is the cost argument against replacing the entire ranking stack with an LLM?
Back: 50M queries/day * $0.007/query (LLM on all) = $10.5M/month vs $450K/month for classical (20x cost increase). LLM yields <5% quality improvement on queries with behavioral data. Use LLMs where behavioral data fails (cold-start, semantic mismatch); classical where it excels (calibrated scoring at scale).

Front: How does cold-start item bootstrapping work with LLMs?
Back: (1) LLM content embedding: process description -> embedding -> immediate ANN retrieval participation. (2) Attribute extraction: LLM extracts structured attributes for ranking model. (3) Similar-item transfer: find semantically similar items with history, transfer signals. (4) Contextual bandits: explore with throttled exposure, learn from feedback.

Front: How do you prevent a cold-start item from being over-recommended based on embedding similarity?
Back: Never give full exposure based on embedding alone. Use quality priors (seller score, listing completeness) as gates. Explore with throttling: expose to 1% of eligible traffic. If engagement exceeds threshold within 48h, increase. If not, suppress.

Front: What is the two-tower contrastive loss (InfoNCE)?
Back: L = -log(exp(sim(q, i+)/tau) / (exp(sim(q,i+)/tau) + sum_j exp(sim(q,i_j-)/tau))). Temperature tau controls softness. In-batch: for batch size B, each positive serves as negative for all other queries (B-1 free negatives per pair).

Front: What is the dot-product limitation of two-tower models?
Back: Interaction reduces to a single scalar from d=128 dimensions. Token-level alignment is lost -- "buy red shoes" and "review red shoes" produce similar embeddings despite radically different intents. Production compromise: two-tower for retrieval over 100M+, cross-attention for scoring on reduced set.

Front: What is DLRM (Deep Learning Recommendation Model)?
Back: Meta's DLRM (Naumov et al., 2019) defines the embedding table + interaction + MLP architecture now standard in industry. Sparse features go through embedding tables, dense features through bottom MLP, interaction layer combines them, top MLP produces prediction.

Front: What is Factorization Machines (FM) and why does it work with sparse features?
Back: FMs factorize interaction weight matrix into low-rank embeddings: W_ij = <v_i, v_j>. Even feature pairs that never co-occur get a learned interaction weight via their embeddings. Critical for sparse recommendation data where most user-item pairs are unobserved.

Front: How does DCN V2's cross layer formula work?
Back: x_{l+1} = x_0 * (W_l * x_l + b_l) + x_l. Element-wise multiplication with x_0 enables explicit feature crossing. Each layer adds one order of interaction. Low-rank W_l and mixture-of-experts allow different interaction patterns per input subspace.

Front: What is the multi-task learning shared-bottom architecture for ranking?
Back: Shared embedding layers feed task-specific towers producing P(click), P(convert), P(long_dwell), P(share). A context-dependent combination policy (e.g., multiplicative: score = P(click)^a * P(convert)^b) merges predictions. Used at YouTube (Zhao et al., 2019).

Front: What is "Pareto regression" and why should you monitor for it?
Back: A Pareto regression is when one objective improves but another degrades without justification (e.g., CTR up but diversity down). It indicates the optimization is trading off objectives rather than improving the frontier. Should trigger review of the ranking policy.

Front: When would you still prefer DeepFM over DCN V2?
Back: When feature space is moderate (<1000 features), training data is limited, and second-order interactions suffice. DeepFM is simpler, faster to train, less prone to overfitting on small datasets. DCN V2 shines with large feature spaces and abundant data.

Front: What is feature hashing in FTRL and why are collisions acceptable?
Back: With billions of possible feature crosses, explicit enumeration is impossible. Hash(feature_name) -> bucket_id in fixed-size array. Collisions acceptable because: (1) L1 regularization zeros out low-signal colliding features, (2) collision rate at 2^24 buckets is <0.1%.

Front: What are the key observability metrics for a production recommendation system?
Back: Online CTR negative delta >0.5% for 24h (ranking regression). Online CVR any regression 48h (P0). Calibration ECE >0.03 (recalibrate). Retrieval Recall@100 <85% (embedding/index issue). Catalog coverage 7-day <40% (filter bubble). LLM reranking lift <2% (remove LLM stage).

Front: How do you debug "CTR improves +3% but CVR drops -1.5%"?
Back: Segment by intent: high-intent queries ("buy X") lost CVR while low-intent improved. Root cause: model trained with CTR objective only ranks "engaging" (clickbait) items higher. Fix: multi-objective loss (CVR for high-intent, CTR for low) or constrained optimization preventing CTR from regressing CVR.

Front: What is the empirical impact of progressive negative sampling improvements?
Back: Random negatives: Recall@100 = 0.45. + In-batch (no correction): 0.52 (+7pts). + Log-Q correction: 0.55 (+3pts). + Hard negative mining: 0.61 (+6pts). Gains from better negatives frequently exceed gains from architecture changes.

Front: What is the DSSM to LLM evolution in retrieval?
Back: DSSM (2013): word hashing -> MLP -> embedding -> cosine sim. Two-tower (2016): feature embedding -> DNN -> embedding -> dot product. LLM-enhanced (2023+): offline LLM(item_text) -> dense embedding -> index, plus two-tower retrieval + LLM reranking on top-K.

Front: What is the "recommendation-as-language" paradigm?
Back: Zhu et al. propose treating user-item interactions as language sequences: "[USER] watched [ITEM_A], bought [ITEM_B], searched [QUERY] -> recommend [?]". LLM understanding enables reasoning about intent. Limitation: slow inference, can't generalize to new items not in training.

Front: What is the practical LLM integration architecture for production recommendation?
Back: LLM generates item embeddings offline (one-time cost), indexed alongside behavioral embeddings. Retrieval blends both sources. Cold-start items: LLM embeddings only path. Rich behavioral data: behavioral embeddings dominate. Captures 80-90% of LLM quality at 1/100th runtime cost.

Front: What is doubly-robust estimation for position bias?
Back: Combines IPW with an imputation model (predicts what the click would have been). Bias from imputation errors is corrected by IPW; variance from extreme IPW weights is bounded by the imputation model. Better than either alone, especially for rarely-shown items.

Front: Why does standard A/B testing fail for marketplace interventions?
Back: Treatment changes auction dynamics for control (SUTVA violation). If treatment group gets better recommendations, they buy items that become unavailable for control. Double-randomized experimentation or interleaving provides trustworthy measurement for marketplace effects.

Front: What is the highest-leverage improvement in recommendation: better models or better training data?
Back: Better training data. Hard negative mining, position bias correction (IPW), and calibration together yield more lift than architecture changes alone. The model learns what the data teaches -- better data (debiased, with hard distinctions) > fancier architecture.

Front: What is the cost optimization priority stack for LLM in recommendation?
Back: (1) Selective LLM routing (20% traffic): 5-10x savings vs full coverage. (2) Offline LLM features (amortize per item): 100x vs real-time per query. (3) Model distillation: 2-3x inference cost. (4) Result caching: 1.3-1.5x. (5) Batch pre-computation for returning users: 1.2x.

Front: When does the Position-Based Model (PBM) assumption break?
Back: (1) Examination depends on the item (attractive thumbnails examined regardless of position). (2) Context effects (previous items affect attention to next). (3) Heterogeneous users (some scroll deeply, some don't). Extensions needed: cascading models, user-specific propensities, doubly-robust estimators.

Front: What is the seniority signal difference for "we use a two-tower model"?
Back: Staff: "We use a two-tower model." Principal/DE: "Two-tower for retrieval, cross-attention for scoring. Dot product is sufficient for recall at scale but loses fine-grained intent matching. Cross-attention on top-200 captures token-level alignment."

Front: What is Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF)?
Back: He et al. (2017) replaced matrix factorization's dot product with neural architecture, proving non-linear user-item interactions improve recommendation. Foundation for moving from linear MF to deep learning in collaborative filtering.

Front: What is the Yi et al. sampling bias correction formula?
Back: L_corrected = -log(exp(s(q,i+)) / (exp(s(q,i+)) + sum_j exp(s(q,i_j-) - log(p_j)))). Subtracting log(p_j) from negative logits ensures the loss is unbiased with respect to a uniform item distribution, regardless of actual sampling frequencies.

Front: What is the Zhao et al. YouTube multi-objective system?
Back: RecSys 2019: shared-bottom multi-task architecture predicts click, watch-time, satisfaction, freshness. Context-dependent combination policy merges predictions (can vary by user segment). Production multi-task learning at scale with learned objective weights.
